scenes.headline: File I/O & File Systems
scenes.subtitle: Reading, writing, and navigating files safely
scenes.narration: Almost every data pipeline begins and ends by touching a file, so mastering how Python reads, writes, and manages them cleanly is foundational work.

scenes.headline: Core file operations
items: open(path, mode) returns a file object
Iterate the file to stream line by line
Always close, or use a with block
scenes.narration: The open call is your gateway to a file, and it hands back an object you interact with. The mode string signals intent, because opening for write truncates a file while append preserves it, and mixing them up destroys data. Iterating the file object streams it one line at a time, which lets you process gigabytes without ever loading everything into memory. Finally, an unclosed handle leaks operating-system resources, so closing is not optional.

scenes.headline: The with statement
scenes.code:
with open('data.csv', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    for line in f:
        process(line.strip())
# file auto-closed here, even on error
scenes.narration: The with block opens the file and binds it to f for the duration of the indented body. Because it is a context manager, it guarantees the file is closed the moment the block exits, whether the loop finishes normally or an exception is raised partway through. Naming encoding='utf-8' explicitly avoids surprises from platform-dependent defaults. This single pattern eliminates the most common source of leaked file handles.

scenes.headline: os.path vs pathlib
scenes.narration: The older os.path module treats paths as plain strings, so you glue segments together with join calls and manipulate them by hand. The modern pathlib module models a path as a rich Path object, letting you build routes with the intuitive slash operator and call methods like exists or read_text directly. Reach for pathlib in any new code, and keep os.path only when maintaining older projects that already depend on it.

scenes.headline: Safe write pattern
scenes.narration: You start by opening the file in write or append mode, then send your data with write calls. Crucially, those writes land in an in-memory buffer first rather than going straight to disk. It is only when the buffer flushes, either explicitly or automatically when the with block exits, that your data is actually persisted.

scenes.text: Always use with open(...) and set encoding='utf-8' to avoid handle leaks and platform bugs.
scenes.narration: Two small habits prevent the overwhelming majority of file bugs: always wrap file access in a with block, and always name your encoding explicitly.
